# Renderers

Turning a scene into pixels on a Vulkan device. Three renderers live in `afield.four.fabricated`, and they disagree about what a frame costs.

**`StandardRenderer` is the one that runs at frame rate.** A small deferred renderer — g-buffer, shadow map, ambient occlusion, lighting composite — built on the `afield.four` primitives rather than hiding them, so you feed it meshes and wire a `RenderTarget` around the passes it hands back. `FabricateFrameGraph` is that pass list made ordered and named, and it does not hide the underlying `Target` objects: inserting a pass and manipulating one directly are both available. `FabricatePostStack` and `FabricatePassChain` are the two post-processing surfaces, and they differ in one thing: a `FabricatePostStack` pass inherits its source's resolution and format, while a `FabricatePassChain` lets every pass declare its own, which is what a half-resolution reduce or a downsample pyramid needs.

**`PathTracingRenderer` is the one that converges.** A progressive GPU path tracer with a stackless software BVH that works on every Field Vulkan device and KHR ray queries where the device has them. It accumulates: the image improves while nothing moves, camera motion resets or reprojects that history, and a lighting edit always starts again. Its scene and environment are snapshots — `PathTraceScene` and `PathTraceEnvironment` are read once at construction, so editing a material means building a new tracer rather than mutating a live one. Output is a fixed-resolution linear HDR render target, and `blitToScreen` is a separate call because exposure and tone mapping are a presentation decision. `PathTraceGltf` loads glTF into it, sRGB-decoding base colour while leaving metallic-roughness linear.

**`GaussianSplatRenderer` is the one that renders something measured rather than modelled.** Splats from a capture, sixteen floats each, sorted and blended rather than rasterized as triangles; `SplatSequence` reads a directory of `.compressed.ply` frames in any order through a bounded most-recently-used cache, because scrubbing a shot is random access and a forward-only reader would be no use for working.

Underneath all three sits `FabricateScene`, a Three.js-shaped scene graph that owns no Vulkan resources at all: nodes carry transforms, renderables carry material and rendering intent, and `FabricateScenePlanner` turns that into the opaque, alpha-masked and back-to-front transparent draw queues a renderer consumes. That independence is what lets the scene graph, the pass graph and the render plan be exercised without a GPU: `FabricateSceneGraphTestMain`, `FabricatePassGraphTestMain` and `FabricateRenderPlanTestMain` are plain `main`s that do, carrying their own assertions. They are not in the `FIELD_TEST` smoke catalog, so run them by hand.

Two constraints apply to the renderers themselves. A renderer is constructed, installed and closed on Field's render thread, like any other `afield.four` module — installing under a name already in use retires the previous occupant, so there is no coroutine lifetime bookkeeping to do. And a device is required: nothing here that draws does so into an `FLine`, or in a headless test, the way the `Math` page's contents do. For the same ground with pictures, see [The Fabricate renderer](../fabricate_renderer.md), [Path tracing](../path_tracing.md) and [afield.four graphics](../afield_four_graphics.md).

## FabricateFrameGraph.kt { #fabricateframegraph-kt }

The renderer's off-screen passes as a named, ordered list, and the one place that order is
written into a `RenderTarget`.

A `StandardRenderer.Bundle` holds its five built-in passes as five separate fields, which is a
set rather than a sequence. [`FabricateFrameGraph`](renderers.md#fabricateframegraph-kt-fabricateframegraph) takes a bundle and makes it a sequence:
g-buffer, shadow map, ambient occlusion, lighting, transparent composite, then one entry for
each effect currently in the bundle's [`FabricatePostStack`](renderers.md#fabricatepoststack-kt-fabricatepoststack). Every built-in name is a constant on
the companion, and `passNameFor` supplies the two that arrive as post effects rather than as
bundle fields, motion blur and anti-aliasing; anything else is named after its effect. So
`insertAfter("my-pass", PASS_LIGHTING, target)` works without knowing how the bundle was built.

`attachTo` is where the order stops being advisory. A `RenderTarget` renders its `preTargets`
before its own pass and in map order, so attaching removes and re-adds every pass by name, which
leaves `preTargets` iterating in the graph's order. It also remembers, per target, which names
this graph put there last time and drops the ones that have since gone, while a pass some other
code added under a name this graph never used is left alone. Attaching a second time is
therefore a resync rather than a duplicate.

The graph is a view. `StandardRenderer.Bundle.frameGraph()` builds a fresh one on each call, it
does not own the targets it names, and it does not stop a box reaching past it to a
`RenderToTexture` directly.

## FabricateMaterialLibrary.kt { #fabricatemateriallibrary-kt }

The flattened per-material record a render queue carries, and the table that hands out its ids.

[`FabricateMaterial`](renderers.md#fabricatescene-kt-fabricatematerial) is the authoring shape: nineteen fields, six of them texture handles.
[`FabricateMaterialRecord`](renderers.md#fabricatemateriallibrary-kt-fabricatematerialrecord) is nine fields wide, and `toRecord` is the conversion. It keeps
base colour, metallic, roughness, alpha cutoff, alpha mode and double-sidedness as they are,
turns `receiveAo` into a 0-or-1 occlusion scale, and leaves the textures, clearcoat, the UV
transform, `receiveShadow` and `sortOrder` behind. Two of the record's fields are placeholders
rather than conversions: `emissive` is written as zero instead of the material's
`emissiveFactor`, and `textureMask` as 0.

[`FabricateMaterialLibrary`](renderers.md#fabricatemateriallibrary-kt-fabricatemateriallibrary) keys materials by identity rather than by equality, so a material
shared between nodes gets one id and two materials with matching values get two. An id is a
position in a dense list, which is why `record(id)` is a plain index and `clear()` invalidates
every id handed out before it. `idFor` converts a material the first time it sees one and
returns the existing id afterwards without re-reading it; `refresh` re-reads into the same slot.
[`FabricateScenePlanner`](renderers.md#fabricaterenderplan-kt-fabricatesceneplanner) keeps a library and calls `refresh` for each visible renderable as it
plans, so [`FabricateRenderPlan`](renderers.md#fabricaterenderplan-kt-fabricaterenderplan)'s `materials` list is current for the frame it was planned in,
and each item's `materialId` indexes it.

## FabricatePassChain.kt { #fabricatepasschain-kt }

The vocabulary for declaring a chain of post passes that are not all the same shape, and the pure
planner that resolves one.

A chain is a list of [`FabricatePassSpec`](renderers.md#fabricatepasschain-kt-fabricatepassspec). Each spec names its pass, carries its fragment shader,
and says how big it wants to be ([`FabricatePassSize`](renderers.md#fabricatepasschain-kt-fabricatepasssize)), in what format, which earlier pass feeds
its primary sampler, and which other earlier passes it wants bound to named samplers. A size may
be absolute, a fraction of the pass's own input, or a fraction of the texture entering the chain,
which is what lets one chain hold a full-resolution pass, a quarter-resolution blur and a
half-float intermediate.

`FabricatePassChain.plan` turns that list into a [`FabricatePassChainPlan`](renderers.md#fabricatepasschain-kt-fabricatepasschainplan) without making a Vulkan
call: it resolves every target shape and every sampler binding, works out which pass last reads
each pass's output, and puts two passes on the same physical target when their outputs never
overlap in time *and* their shapes match. Being arithmetic and reachability rather than GPU state
is what lets `FabricatePassChainTest` exercise all of it on the CPU, which this layer needs more
than most: a resolution resolved one texel wrong renders a picture that looks entirely plausible.

`FabricatePassChainPlan.report` prints the resolution it arrived at — every pass with its shape,
samplers and target slot, and the memory total against one full-resolution target per pass.

## FabricatePassChainBuilder.kt { #fabricatepasschainbuilder-kt }

Materializes a planned pass chain onto the GPU, through the post stack that already exists.

The division of labour is strict. `FabricatePassChain.plan` decides *everything*: every
resolution, every format, which texture every sampler reads, which passes can share a target.
This file decides *nothing*. It walks the plan and calls
`StandardRenderer.Bundle.addShaderEffect` with sizes already resolved to
`FabricatePassSize.Absolute`, so there is no second, subtly different implementation of the
arithmetic sitting where only a GPU can reach it. That matters more here than it usually would,
because a resolution bug in a pass chain renders a picture that looks *fine*.

The passes land in the same [`FabricatePostStack`](renderers.md#fabricatepoststack-kt-fabricatepoststack) as everything else, so [`FabricateFrameGraph`](renderers.md#fabricateframegraph-kt-fabricateframegraph)
schedules them, the stack's `output()` is the chain's output, `insertBefore` and `remove` still
work on them by name, and a chain composes with `addBloom` and `setToneMapping` rather than
replacing them.

[`FabricateBuiltChain`](renderers.md#fabricatepasschainbuilder-kt-fabricatebuiltchain) comes back holding the plan, the built effects and the chain input, and is
how a push constant is retuned afterwards without a rebuild or a reallocation.

## FabricatePassGraph.kt { #fabricatepassgraph-kt }

The ordered, name-keyed map both of this package's pass collections are built on.

[`FabricatePassGraph`](renderers.md#fabricatepassgraph-kt-fabricatepassgraph) is a `LinkedHashMap` with an API that makes the ordering part of the
contract rather than a property of whichever map a caller happened to reach for. Names are
unique and non-blank, and the three ways of putting one in differ in what they will accept:
`addLast` refuses a name already present, `replace` refuses one that is not, and `putOrReplace`
takes either. `insertBefore` and `insertAfter` position a new pass relative to one already
there, and both rebuild the map end to end, because a `LinkedHashMap` has no way to place an
entry anywhere but last.

Two collections here are this map with a type argument and a vocabulary on top.
[`FabricatePostStack`](renderers.md#fabricatepoststack-kt-fabricatepoststack) holds [`FabricatePostEffect`](renderers.md#fabricatepoststack-kt-fabricateposteffect)s, which is what lets a feature insert a post
pass beside one it did not add; [`FabricateFrameGraph`](renderers.md#fabricateframegraph-kt-fabricateframegraph) holds `afield.four` targets, which is what
gives the renderer's off-screen passes names and an order before any of them reach a
`RenderTarget`. Nothing in this file imports anything, so the ordering rules can be exercised on
plain strings, which is what `FabricatePassGraphTestMain.kt` does.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/four/fabricated/FabricatePassGraph.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/four/fabricated/FabricatePassGraph/)

## FabricatePassLibrary.kt { #fabricatepasslibrary-kt }

Worked multi-resolution passes, as lists of [`FabricatePassSpec`](renderers.md#fabricatepasschain-kt-fabricatepassspec) ready to hand to a chain.

Six recipes and two chains assembled from them: a downsample pyramid, a separable Gaussian blur, a
disc aperture blur, an upsample-and-add, a bright pass and a composite, then
`FabricatePassLibrary.apertureChain` and `FabricatePassLibrary.bloomPyramid`. Every one returns
specs rather than touching the GPU, so a chain can be composed from several of them, planned,
printed and asserted on before anything is allocated, and a caller can splice a rung, reorder one
or drop one.

Four of the fragment shaders live here as string constants; the separable blur reuses the nine-tap
kernel the bloom chain already ships rather than keeping a second copy in step with it. All of
them follow the post-stack conventions: a fullscreen triangle, `vUv` texel-aligned so `v = 0` is
image row 0, the primary input bound as `sourceTex`, and every offset scaled by the source's texel
size, so a pass reads its input's texels rather than assuming its own resolution matches.

## FabricatePostEffects.kt { #fabricateposteffects-kt }

High-level post-processing helpers for `StandardRenderer.Bundle`, layered on top of the ordered
[`FabricatePostStack`](renderers.md#fabricatepoststack-kt-fabricatepoststack). These are the "make HDR look right" and "make emissive glow" effects that
Three.js users expect from an EffectComposer: tone mapping + exposure, and bloom.

All passes are built with `StandardRenderer.Bundle.addShaderEffect`, so they chain automatically
(each samples the previous stack output as `sourceTex`). Build the post stack once, then call
`bundle.attachTo(renderer)` so the new passes are synced into the window's frame graph.

## FabricatePostStack.kt { #fabricatepoststack-kt }

The ordered post-processing stack a Fabricate pass lands in, and the record describing one pass.

One source texture enters the stack, named passes run in order, and the last one's target is the
image to present; a stack with no passes presents its input unchanged. Ordering is delegated to
[`FabricatePassGraph`](renderers.md#fabricatepassgraph-kt-fabricatepassgraph), so passes are addressed by name: a feature can insert before or after a pass
it did not add, and two features that each append a pass compose rather than overwriting one
another.

[`FabricatePostEffect`](renderers.md#fabricatepoststack-kt-fabricateposteffect) is what the stack stores: a name, the target the pass renders into, the
module holding its pipeline, and a kind tag. That tag is how [`FabricateFrameGraph`](renderers.md#fabricateframegraph-kt-fabricateframegraph) recognises the
two passes with a fixed place in the standard pass order, motion blur and anti-aliasing; every
other pass is named after its effect.

## FabricateRenderPlan.kt { #fabricaterenderplan-kt }

Render queue data structures and the `FabricateScenePlanner` that builds them from a `FabricateScene`.

The planner walks the scene graph, assigns each visible renderable to one of three queues based
on its material's `alphaMode` (`Opaque`, `AlphaMask`, or `Transparent`), and sorts each queue
for correct draw ordering: opaque and masked items front-to-back by sort order, transparent
items back-to-front by camera distance. Shadow casters are collected from the opaque and masked
sets. `FabricateScene.planScene` calls the planner; `StandardRenderer.Bundle.applyScenePlan`
consumes the resulting `FabricateRenderPlan`.

## FabricateScene.kt { #fabricatescene-kt }

The scene graph: nodes, transforms, materials, lights, animation playback, and the glTF import
that fills them.

This file owns no Vulkan resources and imports no device type, which is a constraint rather than
an accident. A `FabricateNode` carries a transform and children; a renderable carries a
`FabricateMaterial` and the intent to be drawn; `updateWorldTransforms` composes the hierarchy
into world matrices. None of that needs a GPU, so the scene graph, the animation sampler and the
draw-order planning in `FabricateRenderPlan.kt` are all exercisable from a plain `main` — which
`FabricateSceneGraphTestMain` and `FabricateSceneTestMain` do, without a device.

`FabricateTransform` is a position/rotation/scale triple rather than a matrix, and that asymmetry
has bitten callers: handing the graph a composed `Matrix4f` is not enough on its own, so
`FabricateTransform.set(Matrix4f)` decomposes it back into the triple. A transform that cannot
be expressed as one — a shear — will not survive the round trip.

Lights are a list, and an empty list is not the same as no lighting: it preserves the single
default directional light Fabricate has always had, so scenes written before the list existed
render unchanged. One shadow-casting directional light is treated as the key light and drives the
shadow map; the rest reach the deferred lighting pass through a lights buffer.

`FabricateAlphaMode` is the field that decides which of the three draw queues a renderable joins,
and it is the same OPAQUE/MASK/BLEND distinction glTF makes, carried through rather than
collapsed.

Directional lights model the sun (parallel rays, no falloff); point lights radiate from a position with inverse-square falloff clamped by `range`; spot lights add a cone defined by `innerConeDegrees`/`outerConeDegrees`. Only one directional light with `castShadow` can drive the shadow map at a time (the first such light wins); the rest are shaded without shadows.

## FabricateShaderBoxes.kt { #fabricateshaderboxes-kt }

Expose Fabricate's built-in shaders the same way user-authored shaders work: each pass becomes an
editable box with `vertex`/`fragment` GLSL tabs, live introspection, and `alt r` hot reload.

Nothing here is new low-level machinery — it reuses `Box.attachShader`, which installs the reload
actions, copies the module's source into the box's editable properties, and (through `reloadShader`)
rebuilds by copying the module's existing `Parameters`, so the renderer's own `textureResolver`,
attachment formats, and push-constant seeding survive every edit. Only the GLSL source changes.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/four/fabricated/FabricateShaderBoxes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/four/fabricated/FabricateShaderBoxes/)

## GaussianSplatRenderer.kt { #gaussiansplatrenderer-kt }

Rendering a Gaussian splat capture: PLY reading, packing, depth sorting and the built-in
splat shaders.

Splats are not triangles and the differences drive the whole file. Each one is an anisotropic
Gaussian — position, a covariance, colour and opacity, sixteen floats — drawn as a screen-aligned
quad whose falloff the fragment shader evaluates, and the result is only correct if the quads
arrive in depth order, because alpha blending does not commute. So a frame here is a sort
followed by a draw, and most of the machinery below exists to make the sort affordable:
`SortMode.ExactRadix` runs a GPU radix sort over per-splat depth keys, `DepthBuckets` trades
exactness for a cheaper bucketed approximation, and `None` builds none of it, which is the right
answer when the data was written back-to-front already or the blend is order-independent.

A `Cloud` is sized by capacity rather than by the data it was built from, so one cloud can be
rewritten every frame from different files. That is what makes a splat *sequence* playable at
all — see `SplatSequence.kt` for the frame cache on the disk side — and it is why a fifteen-source
frame is one upload into one pre-sized buffer instead of fifteen allocations.

`configureModule` sets the raster state the built-in shaders need and does not set the shader
source, because a box using `moduleHere` owns its vertex and fragment text through its own
properties. That is the seam `simpleGaussianSplatSupport.kt` uses to hand a box an editable
copy of the shaders.

## PathTraceGltf.kt { #pathtracegltf-kt }

glTF and GLB into a [`PathTraceScene`](renderers.md#pathtracescene-kt-pathtracescene): hierarchy baked to world space, PBR parameters mapped onto
[`PathTraceMaterial`](renderers.md#pathtracescene-kt-pathtracematerial), and an extension check that refuses rather than renders the wrong thing.

The tracer has no scene graph — it holds world-space triangles — so this importer flattens the
glTF node hierarchy as it reads, composing each node's transform with the caller's. Textures are
copied out and every Assimp resource is released before the call returns, which is why no
renderer or device is involved and an import is testable from a plain `main`.

Two behaviours are easier to find here than to rediscover from a wrong picture. The first is that
the extension set is read from the JSON directly, ahead of Assimp: an extension in
`extensionsRequired` that this importer does not implement fails the call, while one in
`extensionsUsed` produces a warning and an import of the base material. Declining to load is the
right answer for the former because a required extension means the asset is wrong without it.
The second is that the import is all-or-nothing — geometry accumulates into a staging scene and
is appended only on success, so a failure leaves the target scene exactly as it was rather than
half-populated.

Colour space is the detail that most often looks like a renderer bug. Base colour and emission
textures are sRGB and are decoded; metallic-roughness and normal maps are linear data and are
not. Vertex colours and the base colour factor multiply after decoding, alpha is never squared,
and `PathTraceGltfGpuSmoke` pins all of it against known byte values through real GPU traversal.

## PathTraceGpuSmoke.kt { #pathtracegpusmoke-kt }

GPU smoke tests and a demo entry point for `PathTracingRenderer`.

`PathTraceGpuSmoke.run` sets up known scenes (a constant HDR environment, emissive quads, a
white-furnace diffuse surface, and glass slabs) and reads back linear pixels from real GPU
dispatches to assert accumulation behaviour, lighting and camera resets, HDR material
correctness, Beer-Lambert attenuation, Fresnel, indirect clamping, and transparent-background
compositing. Where the device supports ray queries, both the compute-BVH and ray-query backends
run, and their pixel outputs are compared.

`PathTraceGpuSmoke.runCamera` covers the thin-lens model: pinhole sharpness, aperture blur,
focus-distance changes, pixel jitter, and accumulation invalidation on target or parameter change.

`PathTraceDemo.install` builds a three-sphere scene (diffuse, metallic, rough metal over a floor)
and returns a live `PathTracingRenderer` for interactive use from a box.

## PathTraceInstrument.kt { #pathtraceinstrument-kt }

The path tracer's instrument: what it is doing, why it restarted, and how fast it is converging.

Answering any of that from a box by hand means a `frames { repeat(180) { frame() } }` loop with a
`println` inside: it costs frames of its own, it misses a reset that lands between frame
boundaries, and it cannot see the camera basis the tracer actually built. What is here instead is
a `.h` printer, a `.h2` drill-down and [`PathTraceConvergence`](renderers.md#pathtraceinstrument-kt-pathtraceconvergence), which the tracer appends to from
its own render. Recompiling the integrator in place, the other thing such a loop gets written
for, is `PathTracingRenderer.reloadIntegrator`.

### The two renderings

`registerPathTraceInstrument` gives [`PathTracingRenderer`](renderers.md#pathtracingrenderer-kt-pathtracingrenderer) both an `afield.registerValuePrinter`
and an `afield.registerH2Value` entry, because the class is not a data class and reflection alone
serves the two panels unevenly. `H2Reflect` reflects any type, so `.h2` reaches every public
tuning property without help; `.h` with no printer falls through to `ValueVisualizer`'s
`formatFallbackObject`, which prints the class name and an identity hash and nothing else — while
the `afield.four` types the tracer is *built out of* (`Renderer`, `Camera`,
`ComputeModulePointer`, `RenderToTexture`, `VulkanBuffer`, …) all have printers in
`FourVisualizers.kt`.

So the two renderings do different jobs, and the split is why the `.h` panel stays short:

 - **`.h`** is the glance. One header line and a handful of rows, with the rows that are at their
   defaults *dropped* — so a plain tracer shows five rows, and each of the five optional groups
   (a non-agreeing up, a lens, temporal reuse, fog, an attached convergence log) costs one more,
   to a maximum of ten. It is meant to fit in the gap above the next box.
 - **`.h2`** is the drill-down. A strict superset of what reflection reaches on its own: the same
   values, grouped rather than flat, with the derived facts beside them and the sub-objects still
   reachable so each one lands on its own printer.

### The fact reflection cannot reach

The tracer does not use `camera.up`. `updateFrame` builds its own up as `right × forward`, i.e.
the part of the declared up that is perpendicular to the view direction, normalised, and that is
what reaches the `Frame` uniform. A declared up of `(0, 3, 0)`, or one tilted 20° out of the view
plane, gives a *different* vector from the one the image is built with, and no property tree can
show it, because the value is a local inside a private method. [`PathTraceCameraBasis`](renderers.md#pathtraceinstrument-kt-pathtracecamerabasis) computes
both and reports the angle between them, and the `.h` row appears only when they disagree.

## PathTraceScene.kt { #pathtracescene-kt }

What the path tracer traces: triangles, materials, textures and an environment map, all as plain
Kotlin with no device attached.

Nothing in this file needs a GPU, which is why it is separate from
`PathTracingRenderer.kt`. A scene is assembled by calling `triangle`, `quad`, `mesh` or `sphere`,
each of which appends to flat lists and returns the scene so calls chain; `material` and
`texture` intern a value and hand back the integer index the triangles refer to it by. `pack`
then flattens the result into the float and int arrays the shader expects, and building a BVH
over them is the renderer's job, not this file's. The consequence for a test is that scene
construction, indexing and packing are all checkable headlessly, which is what
`PathTraceTestMain` does.

`PathTraceMaterial` is linear-light throughout — no sRGB anywhere in the struct — and carries
the transmission parameters as well as the metallic-roughness ones, so glass is a material rather
than a separate path. Its one geometric precondition is worth reading before debugging a dark
result: solid (non-thin-walled) glass assumes closed, outward-wound, non-overlapping meshes,
because the attenuation distance is measured between surface crossings.

`PathTraceEnvironment` is both the sky and, usually, the main light. It builds the importance
distribution the sampler draws from, which is why an environment is a snapshot like the geometry
is: changing it changes a precomputed table. `PathTraceTexture` decodes through stb_image and
TinyEXR and keeps its pixels linear, sRGB-decoding base colour while leaving
metallic-roughness alone — the asymmetry glTF requires, and the one
`PathTraceGltfGpuSmoke` checks against known byte values.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/four/fabricated/PathTraceScene.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/four/fabricated/PathTraceScene/)

**Used in:** [Progressive path tracing](../path_tracing.md), [A polytope, cut open, and traced](../chain_polytope_render.md)

## PathTraceTriMesh.kt { #pathtracetrimesh-kt }

[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) into [`PathTraceScene`](renderers.md#pathtracescene-kt-pathtracescene), so that anything in Field which produces a mesh can be traced.

`PathTraceScene.mesh` already takes indexed positions, so the arithmetic here is small. The
difference is what it does with the triangles a real producer emits and
`PathTraceScene.triangle` rejects: zero-area slivers where two vertices coincide, and vertex
normals that came out of a degenerate face as zero-length. A Conway operator chain, a
marching-cubes surface, a Manifold Boolean and a cloth simulation all produce some, and one of
them aborts the whole append. Here they are counted and skipped, and the count comes back in
`PathTraceTriMeshImport.degenerateCount`.

The producers whose output lands here:

| source | route |
| --- | --- |
| a polytope, including Conway chains | `afield.stdlib.polytope.triangulate` `.mesh` |
| a Manifold solid, after Booleans | `afield.manifold.Solid.toTriMesh` |
| a scalar field | `afield.stdlib.marchingCubes`, or `afield.manifold.Solid.levelSet` |
| a mesh off disk | `afield.stdlib.readObj` and the rest of `mesh_io.kt` |
| a heightfield, a tube, a revolve | `mesh_generate.kt` |

### Normals decide whether it reads as faceted or smooth

`TriMesh.normals` is optional, and when it is absent every triangle gets its own face normal, so
the surface reads faceted. That is the right look for a polyhedron and the wrong one for a
sphere. Both Manifold and Field's polytope triangulator can supply either: `toTriMesh(normals =
true)` and `triangulate(normals = NormalPolicy.Crease(30.0))` split a vertex per face at a hard
edge and average across a soft one.

Splitting vertices for shading also breaks index-sharing, so the mesh that shades well is not the
one to measure topology on. Take two: the split mesh for the scene, the plain one for
`afield.stdlib.genus` and `afield.stdlib.isWatertight`.

### A material per triangle

The overload taking a `(triangle: Int) -> Int` selector is handed each triangle's index in `mesh`.
That numbering does not close up over a skipped triangle, so it stays lined up with the
per-triangle side tables a producer hands
out: `afield.stdlib.polytope.TriangulatedGeometry.sourceFace` names the polygon a triangle came
from, and its `triangleAttributes` carry whatever the triangulator was asked to record. So a
Conway chain's lineage can pick the material, and a face's provenance becomes something you can
see in the render.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/four/fabricated/PathTraceTriMesh.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/four/fabricated/PathTraceTriMesh/)

## PathTracingRenderer.kt { #pathtracingrenderer-kt }

The path tracer itself: BVH upload, the two traversal backends, accumulation, and the history
reprojection that keeps an image usable while a camera moves.

This is the device-facing half of the path tracing stack, and the only file in it that owns
Vulkan resources. The scene it traces is built elsewhere — `PathTraceScene.kt` holds the
geometry, materials and environment as plain arrays, `PathTraceGltf.kt` fills them from a glTF
file — and arrives here as an immutable snapshot that is packed into device buffers once. That
split is why editing a material means constructing a new tracer: there is no path from a changed
Kotlin value back into the buffers the shader reads.

Two traversal backends compile from the same source. `COMPUTE_BVH` walks a stackless software
BVH and runs on any Vulkan device Field supports, MoltenVK included; `RAY_QUERY` uses
`VK_KHR_ray_query` hardware traversal where the device advertises it. They share the lighting,
material evaluation and accumulation code, so an image should not depend on which one ran, and
`PathTraceGpuSmoke` exists to check that it does not.

The output is a fixed-resolution linear HDR render target rather than something presentable.
Exposure and Reinhard tone mapping happen in a separate `blitToScreen` pass, so that the
accumulated radiance stays readable — `readLinear` is what the smoke tests measure, and
a tone-mapped buffer would have nothing useful in it.

For the same material with pictures, see `public/docs/path_tracing.md`.

Progressive GPU path tracer: stackless software BVH on every Field Vulkan device, optional KHR ray queries. Construct/install/close on Field's render thread, like other afield.four modules. Scene and environment are snapshots; recreate the tracer to edit them. Camera motion resets or optionally reprojects history; lighting edits always reset accumulation. Output is a fixed-resolution linear HDR RTT. Call blitToScreen separately for exposure + Reinhard presentation. Installing under the same name retires the previous tracer; no coroutine lifetime bookkeeping is needed.

## SplatSequence.kt { #splatsequence-kt }

Playing a splat capture over time: the frame reader, the play head, and the box controls that
drive it.

A splat sequence is a directory of per-frame `.compressed.ply` files, and the reason this file
exists separately from `GaussianSplatRenderer.kt` is that the interesting problem is on the disk
side rather than the GPU side. `SplatSequence` reads frames on demand into a bounded
most-recently-used cache, sized in frames rather than bytes, because a working session scrubs:
a 124-frame capture is 44 MB and would fit whole, a five-minute one will not, and a
forward-only reader would make the short case pleasant and the long case impossible. Nothing
prefetches, which is a decision and not an omission — read-ahead only pays during playback, and
doing it properly costs a thread and a drop policy.

`SplatTransport` is the play head and holds no data at all: a frame index, a rate, and the
playing/looping state. Keeping it separate from the reader is what lets the same transport drive
a sequence on disk or a frame set already resident, and its source `fps` is independent of the
display rate, so a 12 fps capture shown at 60 does not become a 60 fps capture.
`Box.transportControls` wires it to a control group, and the `ToHTML` rendering puts the
play head in a box's output where it can be read at a glance.

## standardRenderer.kt { #standardrenderer-kt }

The deferred renderer the rest of Fabricate is arranged around: the pass bundle, its shaders, and
the configuration that sizes them.

This is the largest file in the package and the one to read first, because the objects it returns
are what almost everything else here consumes. `StandardRenderer.build(...)` builds the five
passes — g-buffer, shadow map, ambient occlusion, lighting composite, transparent composite —
and hands back a `Bundle` holding each as an ordinary `afield.four` `Target`, along with the
scene defaults, the scene graph and the post stack. Nothing is hidden
behind that: `FabricateFrameGraph` wraps the same targets to give them names and an order,
`FabricatePostStack` appends to them, and a box that wants to reach past all of it and
manipulate a `RenderToTexture` directly still can. The design decision throughout is to compose
the existing primitives rather than replace them.

Deferred is the choice that explains the pass list. Geometry is rasterized once into a g-buffer
of positions, normals and material parameters, and lighting is then evaluated per screen pixel,
so cost scales with lights rather than with lights times triangles — which is what lets
`FabricateScene`'s light list be arbitrary. It is also why transparency needs a separate pass at
the end: a g-buffer holds one surface per pixel, and a blended surface is a second one.

Scenes are not built here. `FabricateScene` owns the graph and `FabricateScenePlanner` produces
the draw queues; this file renders what it is given. For the renderer working, with captures of
each pass, see `public/docs/fabricate_renderer.md`.

## standardShapes.kt { #standardshapes-kt }

Ten par_shapes primitives, written straight into vertex-pulling buffers as triangle soup.

[`StandardShapes`](renderers.md#standardshapes-kt-standardshapes) is the layer under `StandardRenderer.Bundle.registerCube`, `registerSphere` and
the eight other `register*` shape helpers, one per function here. Each builds a par_shapes mesh,
scales it, translates it if the call gave a centre, and writes it into two buffers the caller
supplies, one for positions and one for normals. The write is **non-indexed**: the source mesh's
triangle list is expanded, so three vertices go out per triangle and a vertex-pulling shader
reads a position and its normal at the same index with no indirection. `ShapeWriteResult` comes
back carrying the source mesh's vertex and triangle counts alongside what was actually written,
which is how a caller sizes its mesh afterwards instead of predicting the triangle count up
front.

`WriteConfig` covers the two decisions a caller usually has to make. `padVec3To4` writes each
vector as four floats for std430 alignment and is on by default; `append` chooses between
continuing after whatever is already in the buffer and starting at its beginning, and all ten
`register*` helpers pass `append = false`. Normals come from par_shapes, computed there if the
mesh arrived without any, with an index that falls outside the normal buffer reading the
triangle's face normal instead. Each call frees its par_shapes mesh before returning.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/four/fabricated/standardShapes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/four/fabricated/standardShapes/)
